The Bank of England has raised interest rates for the first time in three years and warned of another increase to combat inflationary pressure unleashed by the Iran war.

Eight members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) voted for the rise, which takes the base rate from 3.75% to 4%. The ninth member, Catherine Mann, preferred a more dramatic half-point increase.

The Middle East conflict has pushed oil prices persistently above $100 a barrel in recent months, as hopes have evaporated of a deal that could reopen the strait of Hormuz.

As a result, the Bank now expects UK inflation to rise to 4.9% in the middle of next year – up from 3.2% in its last economic forecast in July. Inflation hit 3.5% in September, as measured on the consumer prices index.

The decision, which will hit mortgage borrowers, comes a week after John Healey used his first budget to promise “breathing space” for hard-pressed consumers. Echoing the Office for Budget Responsibility’s gloomy forecasts for living standards, the MPC expects real post-tax income to fall this year and next.

The Bank’s governor, Andrew Bailey, raised the prospect of another rate rise in the near future – with a resolution to the Iran conflict the key factor that will influence the decision.

“Without news which softens the risks to inflationary pressures, I can see the argument for a further increase in rates and thereafter taking a more conditional approach,” he said, according to the MPC minutes.

However, he played down the likelihood of a prolonged series of increases, as markets have been predicting. “Today’s increase shouldn’t be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence in hikes. But unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase,” he said.

The Bank’s next interest rate decision will be announced on 17 December, and some analysts suggested the MPC could press ahead with a pre-Christmas hike.

Andrew Goodwin, the chief economist at consultancy Oxford Economics, said: “The degree of inflationary pressure already in the system means another hike in December or February is likely.”

Explaining its decision to raise borrowing costs, the MPC highlighted the pass-through from elevated oil prices to business and consumer costs across the economy. It expects the Ofgem energy cap to rise from the equivalent of £1,723 a year for an average household in Great Britain to £2,150 in January and to increase again in April. Food price inflation could hit 4.75% by mid-2027, it warned.

Businesses have so far reported in the Bank’s surveys that they have been able to absorb soaring oil and gas prices – by hedging their energy costs, for example – but the MPC believes they will soon have to start passing them on to consumers in higher prices.

It is also concerned about workers seeking to offset the impact of the higher cost of living by asking for bumper pay rises.

Oil prices have fallen sharply, to below $100 a barrel, after the Democrats’ victories in the US Congress, which some investors have interpreted as potentially constraining Donald Trump’s capacity to prolong the conflict in Iran. Trump’s vice-president, JD Vance, has blamed the war, and its impact on inflation, for the rout at the polls.

Speaking at the Bank’s press conference, Bailey welcomed the sharp fall in energy prices in the last 48 hours but said it would need to be sustained to change his view about the need for future rate rises. “This is positive news, but there is already a significant amount of inflationary pressure in the pipeline,” he said, adding: “What is the best thing that can happen? It is to resolve the conflict in the Middle East.”

While the decision to increase rates was supported by all MPC members, the minutes of the meeting reveal stark divisions over how much further they may need to go to bring inflation under control. The dovish Alan Taylor suggested this should be a “risk-management ‘one-for-now’ insurance hike”, while Mann argued that an immediate half-point rise was necessary to restore the Bank’s inflation-fighting credibility.

Healey’s budget included measures aimed at cushioning the impact of higher energy prices – including extending the fuel duty freeze and the VAT cut on electricity bills. The MPC said the package would shave a quarter percentage point off inflation in mid-2027.

Responding to the interest rate increase, Healey said: “The Iran conflict is reaching deep into the pockets of families and businesses here at home.

“In my budget I acted to give some breathing space to families and businesses. Twenty million households will get a £100 energy payment, I extended the tax cut on electricity bills and froze fuel duty. I also set out the course ahead to get costs down for good.”

But the shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, called the rate rise “another headwind for hardworking families to deal with”.

articles.title: ICJ is due to rule on the Rohingya genocide case. Here's what you need to know
articles.summary: ICJ is due to rule on the Rohingya genocide case. Here's what you need to know Submitted by Sondos Asem on Thu, 11/05/2026 - 11:06 UN's top court sets 19 November as date for landmark judgment in case brought by Gambia against Myanmar Off The International Court of Justice (ICJ) will rule on whether Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya , in a judgment that could see the court hold a state responsible for genocide for the first time. Officials announced on Tuesday that the court's president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa, would read the judgment at a public sitting at the Peace Palace in The Hague at 10am local time on 19 November. The ruling will be final and binding, with no right of appeal. Several governments have already described the violence as genocide, including the US and Canada . Legal experts say they expect the outcome to have consequences for other ICJ cases involving allegations of genocide, most pressingly South Africa's case against Israel over its war against Palestinians in Gaza, where the confirmed death toll has reached almost 75,000 people. The case, brought by the Gambia in 2019, concerns the Myanmar military's 2017 violence in Rakhine State, which drove more than 700,000 Rohingya into neighbouring Bangladesh and involved widely documented massacres and rapes. About 1.2 million Rohingya, a predominantly Muslim minority, now live in camps around Cox's Bazar, the world's largest refugee settlement. Myanmar has denied committing genocide, saying its forces were responding to insurgents from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa), whose attacks on police posts in August 2017 killed 12 security personnel. Antonia Mulvey, an international human rights lawyer who investigated sexual violence against the Rohingya for the UN in 2017, told Middle East Eye's Expert Witness Podcast that horrific sexual violence was central to the Gambia's argument that genocide took place. "One individual said to me, 'I was lucky, I was only raped by three men,'" said Mulvey, whose organisation, Legal Action Worldwide, now represents Rohingya witnesses in the case. "They would rape women and girls in public, in front of their family members, in front of their children, in communal areas. I heard of mass gang rapes, sometimes up to 40 women and girls at the time." What is the case about? The Gambia accuses Myanmar of breaching the 1948 Genocide Convention during its campaign against the Rohingya from 25 August 2017. The operations were carried out under Min Aung Hlaing, then the military's commander-in-chief. Myanmar at the time had a civilian government led by Aung San Suu Kyi, but the military-drafted constitution left the armed forces outside its control. In February 2021, Min Aung Hlaing overthrew Suu Kyi's government in a coup, and in April this year he stepped down as army chief. He was later elected president by a parliament dominated by military-backed lawmakers, following elections organised by the junta. Rohingya fled mass killings, rape and the burning of villages during what the military described as "clearance operations". The case is a dispute between states, so the court will decide whether Myanmar as a state is responsible, not whether any individual is guilty. A finding against Myanmar would arguably add to international pressure on Min Aung Hlaing, whose move to the presidency is widely perceived as a bid for international legitimacy. How did it start? In 2018, the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Myanmar concluded that there was sufficient information to infer genocidal intent and recommended that senior military officials be investigated and prosecuted for genocide. On 11 November 2019, the Gambia filed its case at the ICJ with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC). The Rohingya case that could redefine the law on genocide rought a genocide case before the court. The west African country relied on the principle that every state party to the 1948 Genocide Convention has a common interest in seeing it upheld. In December 2019, Aung San Suu Kyi, then Myanmar's civilian leader, appeared at the court to deny the allegations. In January 2020, after finding “ a real and imminent risk of irreparable prejudice to the rights” of the Rohingya under the Genocide Convention, the court ordered Myanmar to prevent genocidal acts and preserve evidence. The court rejected Myanmar's objections to its jurisdiction in July 2022, and heard the merits of the case from 12-29 January 2026, including closed-door testimony from Rohingya witnesses. Eleven states have intervened: Belgium, Canada, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Denmark, France, Germany, the Republic of Ireland, the Maldives, the Netherlands, Slovenia and the United Kingdom. Mike Becker, an assistant professor of international human rights law at Trinity College Dublin and a former associate legal officer at the ICJ, told MEE the judgment would be the first merits judgment in a case with large-scale intervention by third states. "Cases like the Gambia v Myanmar have arguably sought to transform the role and function of the ICJ in contemporary affairs. The outcome here may determine whether that trend will continue," Becker said. What are the arguments? The Gambia argued that genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference to be drawn from the Myanmar military's conduct. It relied on four acts listed in the convention: killing; causing serious bodily or mental harm; inflicting conditions of life calculated to destroy the group; and measures intended to prevent births. Mulvey said the Gambia pointed to around 10,000 killings, which she described as a conservative estimate, and to decades of restrictions on Rohingya marriage, births, movement and access to healthcare. Myanmar denies genocide. It argues the operations were a counterterrorism response to Arsa, that there is no direct evidence of intent, and that the UN fact-finding mission's reports should not be given evidentiary weight. Myanmar has submitted 12 reports on its compliance with the 2020 order. The Gambia has said these give "no reason to conclude" that Myanmar complied. Why is sexual violence central? Mulvey said she documented a consistent pattern across the townships of Maungdaw, Buthidaung and Rathedaung, in which soldiers surrounded villages, opened fire, set homes alight and then selected women and girls for rape. She said survivors described gang rapes carried out in public and in front of their families, women held in military camps for weeks, mutilation, and soldiers telling them: "We will kill you by raping you." One woman told Mulvey she had been eight months pregnant when she was hanged from a tree and raped by nine men, most of them soldiers. Her unborn child died. Her account was included in the fact-finding mission's report and later read out at the ICJ. The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda ruled in 1998 that rape can constitute genocide. The ICJ has accepted the principle, but has never found a state responsible on that basis. Mulvey said such a finding would be "a landmark decision". "It was the scale and the brutality of the sexual violence that we didn't see in previous cases before the International Court of Justice, such as before Bosnia and Croatia," she said. Why does it matter under international law? The judgment will be only the third time the ICJ has ruled on the merits of a genocide case, and the first in more than a decade. In 2007, the court found that genocide was committed at Srebrenica but held Serbia responsible only for failing to prevent and punish it. 'It was the scale and the brutality of the sexual violence that we didn't see in previous cases before the International Court of Justice' – Antonia Mulvey, human rights lawyer In 2015, it found that genocide had not been proven in Croatia's case against Serbia. Furthermore, how the court applies the “only reasonable inference” test is expected to be a central legal question addressed by the judgment. The test governs how genocidal intent, meaning the intent to destroy a group in whole or in part, can be proven when there is no direct evidence of it, such as an explicit order or policy document. In this case, it would require proving whether any explanation other than genocide could reasonably account for what happened in Rakhine. The Gambia argues that the scale, pattern and brutality of the 2017 operations meet that test. It points to the mass killings, the systematic rape of women and girls, and decades of discriminatory policies against the Rohingya. “Here we don’t have a physical document that shows that, but it was the whole pattern that we saw,” Mulvey said. Myanmar argues that other reasonable inferences can be drawn, chiefly that its forces were conducting counterterrorism operations against Arsa. At the January hearings, its counsel also argued that the military’s aim was to drive the Rohingya out of the country, not to destroy them. Chris Sidoti, a former member of the UN fact-finding mission on Myanmar, told MEE that the ruling would also show how the court approaches establishing facts and the weight given to reports from UN human rights mechanisms. "The International Court of Justice is not a fact-finding tribunal. It doesn't have an investigative arm, and mostly it makes decisions that are purely legal questions," said Sidoti, who now sits on the UN Commission of Inquiry on Palestine and Israel. "Here it's got a fact-finding task ahead of it." Will the ICJ lower the genocide threshold? In October, US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz accused Navi Pillay, the Nobel Peace laureate and the ad hoc judge appointed by the Gambia, of "tipping the scales", saying she intended to lower the threshold for proving genocide so it could be used against America and its allies. Mulvey rejected the claim as "misleading". "The Gambia is very clear in its submissions; they are not asking the court to lower the threshold [for genocide]. Rather, they are saying the threshold has been met," she said. What do the victims want? Rohingya survivors want the court to find Myanmar responsible for genocide and to order the return of their land and property, compensation and prosecutions. Above all, they want citizenship, which they are denied under Myanmar's 1982 citizenship law, said Mulvey. If the court finds Myanmar responsible, it will also find that Myanmar must make reparation to the Rohingya, though it may defer the question of remedies to a later phase, Becker said. The remedy the court orders "could be groundbreaking, especially if the ICJ requires Myanmar to undertake domestic reforms to guarantee basic rights of citizenship and non-discrimination to the Rohingya", he said. "Decades on, they don't forget what has happened to them or to their families," Mulvey said. "At the very minimum, they want recognition." What happens next? Myanmar is bound to comply with the judgment. If it does not, the Gambia can refer the matter to the UN Security Council, which has never used its power to enforce an ICJ ruling. Becker said enforcement may prove impossible while the military remains in power, but "compliance with the ICJ judgment may become the price of readmission to the international community". A finding against Myanmar could also increase pressure on other states to disengage from the ICJ, he said. Myanmar has been embroiled in civil war since the 2021 coup, and the Arakan Army, an ethnic armed group, now controls most of Rakhine State. Separately, the prosecutor of the International Criminal Court applied in November 2024 for an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing, then the military's commander-in-chief, over the deportation and persecution of the Rohingya. Judges have not publicly ruled on the request. “We want to see that arrest warrant issued, and also that arrest warrants are requested for other senior members of the Myanmar military,” Mulvey said. In February 2025, a court in Argentina ordered arrest warrants for 25 Myanmar officials, including Min Aung Hlaing and Aung San Suu Kyi, in a case brought under the legal principle that atrocity crimes can be prosecuted anywhere. Because the court relies on precedents as part of its sources, the case will have implications on the other genocide-related cases pending before the ICJ: Ukraine v Russia , South Africa v Israel , Nicaragua v Germany and the Democratic Republic of the Congo v Rwanda . "It was the scale and the brutality of the sexual violence that we didn't see in previous cases before the International Court of Justice, such as before Bosnia and Croatia," she said.

Why does it matter under international law? The judgment will be only the third time the ICJ has ruled on the merits of a genocide case, and the first in more than a decade. In 2007, the court found that genocide was committed at Srebrenica but held Serbia responsible only for failing to prevent and punish it. 'It was the scale and the brutality of the sexual violence that we didn't see in previous cases before the International Court of Justice' – Antonia Mulvey, human rights lawyer In 2015, it found that genocide had not been proven in Croatia's case against Serbia.

Furthermore, how the court applies the “only reasonable inference” test is expected to be a central legal question addressed by the judgment. The test governs how genocidal intent, meaning the intent to destroy a group in whole or in part, can be proven when there is no direct evidence of it, such as an explicit order or policy document. In this case, it would require proving whether any explanation other than genocide could reasonably account for what happened in Rakhine.

The Gambia argues that the scale, pattern and brutality of the 2017 operations meet that test. It points to the mass killings, the systematic rape of women and girls, and decades of discriminatory policies against the Rohingya. “Here we don’t have a physical document that shows that, but it was the whole pattern that we saw,” Mulvey said. Myanmar argues that other reasonable inferences can be drawn, chiefly that its forces were conducting counterterrorism operations against Arsa.

At the January hearings, its counsel also argued that the military’s aim was to drive the Rohingya out of the country, not to destroy them. Chris Sidoti, a former member of the UN fact-finding mission on Myanmar, told MEE that the ruling would also show how the court approaches establishing facts and the weight given to reports from UN human rights mechanisms. "The International Court of Justice is not a fact-finding tribunal.

It doesn't have an investigative arm, and mostly it makes decisions that are purely legal questions," said Sidoti, who now sits on the UN Commission of Inquiry on Palestine and Israel. "Here it's got a fact-finding task ahead of it." Will the ICJ lower the genocide threshold? In October, US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz accused Navi Pillay, the Nobel Peace laureate and the ad hoc judge appointed by the Gambia, of "tipping the scales", saying she intended to lower the threshold for proving genocide so it could be used against America and its allies.

Mulvey rejected the claim as "misleading". "The Gambia is very clear in its submissions; they are not asking the court to lower the threshold [for genocide]. Rather, they are saying the threshold has been met," she said. What do the victims want? Rohingya survivors want the court to find Myanmar responsible for genocide and to order the return of their land and property, compensation and prosecutions.

Above all, they want citizenship, which they are denied under Myanmar's 1982 citizenship law, said Mulvey. If the court finds Myanmar responsible, it will also find that Myanmar must make reparation to the Rohingya, though it may defer the question of remedies to a later phase, Becker said. The remedy the court orders "could be groundbreaking, especially if the ICJ requires Myanmar to undertake domestic reforms to guarantee basic rights of citizenship and non-discrimination to the Rohingya", he said.

"Decades on, they don't forget what has happened to them or to their families," Mulvey said. "At the very minimum, they want recognition." What happens next? Myanmar is bound to comply with the judgment. If it does not, the Gambia can refer the matter to the UN Security Council, which has never used its power to enforce an ICJ ruling. Becker said enforcement may prove impossible while the military remains in power, but "compliance with the ICJ judgment may become the price of readmission to the international community".

A finding against Myanmar could also increase pressure on other states to disengage from the ICJ, he said. Myanmar has been embroiled in civil war since the 2021 coup, and the Arakan Army, an ethnic armed group, now controls most of Rakhine State. Separately, the prosecutor of the International Criminal Court applied in November 2024 for an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing, then the military's commander-in-chief, over the deportation and persecution of the Rohingya.

Judges have not publicly ruled on the request. “We want to see that arrest warrant issued, and also that arrest warrants are requested for other senior members of the Myanmar military,” Mulvey said. In February 2025, a court in Argentina ordered arrest warrants for 25 Myanmar officials, including Min Aung Hlaing and Aung San Suu Kyi, in a case brought under the legal principle that atrocity crimes can be prosecuted anywhere.

Because the court relies on precedents as part of its sources, the case will have implications on the other genocide-related cases pending before the ICJ: Ukraine v Russia , South Africa v Israel , Nicaragua v Germany and the Democratic Republic of the Congo v Rwanda . articles.title: Saudi coalition says it intercepted missile fired at Medina

The Houthis rejected any suggestion they were targeting the city, saying such accusations were a "blatant and grave falsehood". "Our operations target only its oil facilities and military bases," the group said in a statement.

articles.title: Iran signals satisfaction, skepticism after US midterm vote
articles.summary: While the Iranian regime says the US midterms will not change Washington's policy toward Tehran, some officials and commentators see the resounding Democratic victory as blowback against the Iran war.
articles.preview: November 5, 2026 While the Iranian regime says the US midterms will not change Washington's policy toward Tehran, some officials and commentators see the resounding Democratic victory as blowback against the Iran war. Iran's leadership has downplayed the significance of Republican setbacks in the US midterm elections, insisting that the Democratic takeover of Congress is unlikely to alter Washington's policy toward the Islamic Republic.
articles.body:
November 5, 2026

While the Iranian regime says the US midterms will not change Washington's policy toward Tehran, some officials and commentators see the resounding Democratic victory as blowback against the Iran war.

Iran's leadership has downplayed the significance of Republican setbacks in the US midterm elections, insisting that the Democratic takeover of Congress is unlikely to alter Washington's policy toward the Islamic Republic.

"If there are still those who believe that America can be persuaded to abandon its hostility toward the Iranian nation through concessions or partisan changes in the US political system, they are gravely mistaken," Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said in a statement after the vote.

Khamenei also warned that Tehran would respond more forcefully to any future US military action.

The elections took place after months of military confrontation between Tehran and Washington, which disrupted global energy markets and raised fears of a broader regional conflict.

Tehran likely to stick to its course despite US political shift

Mohammad Sadegh Javadi Hesar, Iran-based journalist and member of the reformist party Etemad-e Melli, said the election outcome was unlikely to affect Iran's calculations.

"Iran will not change its position simply because Republicans have lost their majority," he told DW.

According to Javadi Hesar, decisions about ending the conflict will ultimately be made in Washington. Tehran, in turn, is expected to continue insisting on its previous demands for peace, such as the end of all hostilities, including in Lebanon, and the lifting of US naval blockade.

Is a vote for US Democrats a vote against the Iran war?

Others in Iran interpreted the results more positively.

Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf argued that American voters had delivered their verdict on the Iranian conflict.

"The Americans said no to war," Ghalibaf said on X, while acknowledging that rising cost of living also contributed to Donald Trump's party losing the election.

Ghalibaf also mocked US Vice President JD Vance who had acknowledged that the Iran war was the reason the Republicans lost.

"Skip the TED talk. Why not say this to your boss?" Ghalibaf wrote on X.

Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said Iran not only challenged the United States on the battlefield and in the Strait of Hormuz but had also dealt it a political setback in Washington.

Several Iranian media outlets echoed that assessment. The news website Etelaat Online sarcastically suggested that the long-discussed "regime change" had ultimately taken place not in Iran, but in the United States.

Looking back to Jimmy Carter

Some commentators drew historical parallels to another period of US-Iran tension.

The state-affiliated Mehr News Agency compared Trump's political troubles to those of former US President Jimmy Carter, recalling the failed 1980 American military operation to rescue hostages held in Tehran.

At the time, the US deployed eight military helicopters to rendezvous with six transport planes in the Iranian desert before moving on Tehran to free the hostages. However, the aircraft encountered a sand storm and a deadly crash between a helicopter and a C-130 transport plane, killing eight Americans.

The agency argued that the 1980 episode demonstrated the limits of US military power in resolving disputes with Iran. Carter went on to lose the presidential election to Ronald Reagan later that year.

Iran released the hostages in January 1981, just minutes after Reagan was sworn in for his first presidential term.

No winds of change between Iran and US

Hardline media, however, dismissed the election's broader significance.

Tasnim News Agency, which is close to Iran's Revolutionary Guards, argued that there is little meaningful difference between Republicans and Democrats when it comes to Iran policy. According to the agency, both parties pursue similar goals toward the Islamic Republic despite differences in rhetoric.

Using a Persian proverb, Tasnim summed up its view bluntly: "The yellow dog is the brother of the jackal," suggesting that neither side should be expected to act differently toward Iran.

Diplomacy rather than escalation?

Veteran Iranian diplomat Hossein Alizadeh says the actual midterm fallout is difficult to predict, but notes US politics sends ripples out across the entire world.

"The USA is a superpower and a hegemonic power. Consequently, developments in that country are of significance to the entire world — from Mexico and Canada, through the European Union, to China, and, of course, the Middle East," he told DW.

Alizadeh is an expert in international relations who served in the diplomatic corps of the Islamic Republic for 22 years, before resigning in 2010 in protest of the 2009 Iranian post-election crackdown.

The Finland-based analyst considers another large-scale military escalation by the USA to be unlikely. While the Democrats are also opponents of the Islamic Republic, "unlike the Trump administration, they opted for a diplomatic agreement with Tehran. The 2015 nuclear deal placed Iranian nuclear activities under the oversight of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA)," says Alizadeh.

He points out that the Democrats and the US allies were not in favor or attacking Iran.

"The negative repercussions of such a war have already become clear," he told DW.

This piece was originally published in German

articles.title: Can Iran’s new supreme leader make peace from behind the scenes?
articles.summary: Mojtaba Khamenei’s consultations suggest a new system of decision-making is taking shape.
articles.preview: Mojtaba Khamenei’s consultations suggest a new system of decision-making is taking shape, but can it deliver a compromise like the 2015 nuclear deal? Iran’s new supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, is exercising power without appearing in public or allowing his voice to be heard. Since succeeding his father in March, he has governed through written statements and decrees, while reports of his meetings with senior officials offer a glimpse into how he exercises power.
articles.body:
Mojtaba Khamenei’s consultations suggest a new system of decision-making is taking shape, but can it deliver a compromise like the 2015 nuclear deal?

Iran’s new supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, is exercising power without appearing in public or allowing his voice to be heard. Since succeeding his father in March, he has governed through written statements and decrees, while reports of his meetings with senior officials offer a glimpse into how he exercises power.

The meetings announced in May and August appeared intended primarily to reassure Iranians that their new leader was alive and exercising authority. But a series of four meetings announced within 11 days in October, involving the heads of Iran’s parliament, judiciary and national security establishment, as well as senior military commanders, suggests something more: a new system of decision-making taking shape.

The meetings come as Tehran weighs its options between negotiations and renewed confrontation with the United States and Israel. They also invite comparisons with the consultations that preceded the 2015 nuclear agreement. The question is whether Iran’s new leadership is preparing for a similarly consequential decision, and whether this system is capable of making one.

The new Khameneism

For nearly 37 years, Ali Khamenei’s rule rested on his direct personal presence: speeches setting red lines, public meetings with commanders, political elites and ordinary Iranians. His son came to power in different circumstances. Injured in the February 28 strike that killed his father, he was advised, according to sources close to him quoted by Reuters, not to appear or release audio recordings for fear of being tracked.

His rule has taken shape through decrees rebuilding institutions, decisions channelled through a narrow circle of trusted officials, and the testimony of others in place of personal appearances.

The October meetings followed appointments to replace military and security commanders killed in the war. In August, Khamenei appointed his military adviser, Mohsen Rezaei, as his representative on the Supreme National Security Council; Rezaei later became its secretary. Six military appointments followed, including Ali Abdollahi as chief of the Armed Forces General Staff, Ahmad Vahidi as commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and Ali Azmaei as IRGC Navy commander. Abdollahi was also instructed to complete the merger of the General Staff with Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters.

The sequence of Khamenei’s reported meetings is revealing. Those announced in May with President Masoud Pezeshkian and Abdollahi, then head of Khatam al-Anbiya, and another with Pezeshkian announced in August, served chiefly to reassure Iranians that the new leader was alive and exercising his duties. October’s meetings appear to have constituted a systematic round of consultations reaching from constitutional institutions to the armed forces.

At his first reported meeting with the military leadership he had reconstituted, announced on October 31, Abdollahi, army commander Amir Hatami and Vahidi reportedly briefed Khamenei on military readiness in the Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and the Sea of Oman.

Iran thus appears to be moving from reconstruction to operation: activating a decision-making system rather than merely establishing the leader’s presence.

These consultations unfolded alongside intensive mediation, with each stage of internal consultation following an external diplomatic development.

On October 20, Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, carried a Qatari-Pakistani compromise proposal to Tehran. According to Arab media reports, it envisaged unannounced inspections of nuclear facilities in exchange for Iran receiving the interest on its frozen funds in Qatar. Khamenei’s meeting with Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s chief negotiator, was announced the following day.

On October 26, Munir returned with Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman Al Saud and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin. Their discussions produced an understanding that regional security was the responsibility of the region’s own states. Rezaei also announced that Tehran had sent Washington a proposal concerning the Strait of Hormuz with a seven-day deadline. Khamenei’s meeting with Rezaei, who had received a letter from US Vice President JD Vance, was announced the next day.

On October 30, Qatari mediators held 12 hours of talks in Tehran, coordinated with the White House, after US envoy Tom Barrack suggested an initial understanding was close. Khamenei’s meeting with military commanders was announced the following day.

This timing suggests that internal consultation has become the other side of external mediation.

The statements from these meetings carry two parallel, not contradictory, messages. In the meeting with Rezaei, Khamenei insisted on Iran’s conditions for ending the war, escaping the debilitating state of “neither war nor peace” and managing the Strait of Hormuz. In his instructions to the commanders, he demanded immediate retaliation against any threat without geographical limits, an expanded list of US and Israeli targets, and emphasised that Iran would decide when any renewed confrontation ended.

Repeated appeals for unity suggest an awareness of competing views within the political elite over war and negotiations.

Yet the meetings appear to have defined the upper and lower limits of Iran’s choices, rather than settled on a particular course: at one end, rejecting an intolerable continuation of “neither war nor peace”; at the other, preparing to widen the war if attacks resume. Between these limits lie a settlement on Iranian terms, pursued through Ghalibaf, Rezaei and the mediators, or continued mutual pressure while strengthening the domestic front.

The gap remains wide. Washington wants nuclear concessions before negotiations resume; Tehran first wants the naval blockade lifted, frozen assets released and oil exports restored.

Significantly, Khamenei spoke of conditions “set by the country’s officials”, not by himself. The wording distributes responsibility among institutions and preserves room for him to embrace or disown an eventual outcome.

The comparison with 2015

There are echoes here of the lengthy consultations before the nuclear agreement of July 14, 2015.

A secret channel in Muscat opened with Ali Khamenei’s approval. On September 17, 2013, he spoke to IRGC commanders of “heroic flexibility”, reassuring the military before negotiations. In June 2015, he set out his red lines, and in October he issued a letter of conditional approval. Responsibility for the nuclear file passed from the Supreme National Security Council to the Foreign Ministry under Mohammad Javad Zarif, a sign that the political decision had been made.

The resemblance is clear: a supreme leader establishes red lines, delegates negotiations to trusted figures and brings the military into the process before a major shift.

The differences are deeper. The earlier process lasted around two years under sanctions, not war. Today’s consultations were compressed into 11 days amid armed confrontation, a naval blockade and the approaching November 3 US midterm elections.

Ali Khamenei spoke in his own voice; his son speaks through written statements. Diplomats led the earlier negotiations; now two figures with IRGC backgrounds, Ghalibaf and Rezaei, play central roles. Where the earlier backchannel ran through Oman, today mediation involves Qatar and the countries of the Mecca Agreement, signed on August 7.

Above all, “heroic flexibility” was presented to commanders as preparation for an agreement. Today, conditions for a settlement sit alongside an expanded list of military targets.

The deficit of trust has also deepened. If the legacy of 1979 shaped Washington’s view of Tehran, and the US withdrawal from the nuclear agreement in 2018 shaped Tehran’s view of Washington, the wars of June 2025 and February 2026 have added a layer of mistrust that no technical agreement can easily overcome.

The consultations thus resemble those of 2013 in form but not function. Then, they prepared the ground for negotiations; now, they prepare for a choice between negotiation and escalation.

The seven reported meetings suggest that the new Khameneism may be more than an attempt to fill a leadership vacuum. Its decision-making machinery appears to be in place and functioning, even though the supreme leader’s presence can be established only through others.

Yet every announcement intended to dispel doubts produces more of them, without photographs or details of exactly when and where the meetings took place. The legitimacy of decisions remains partly dependent on the legitimacy of the leader’s presence.

Can this system, with its new commanders and parallel messages of compromise and deterrence, make a decision as consequential as the one taken in 2015, when war has raised the political cost of flexibility beyond what a leader who has yet to appear publicly may be able to bear?

The father saw and was seen; the son makes his presence felt through endorsements and influence from behind protective barriers.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: JD Vance distances himself from Trump and Iran war after US midterms debacle
articles.summary: United States Vice-President JD Vance distanced himself from Donald Trump's defence of the Iran war after the Republican party's debacle in the midterm elections.
articles.preview: USA United States Vice President JD Vance publicly broke from President Donald Trump's defence of the Iran war Wednesday after the Republican Party's deep losses in the midterm elections, attempting to distance himself from voters' clear rebuke of the president as the vice president faces questions about his own political ambitions. Vance, who has said he would decide after the election whether to run for president in 2028, issued a lengthy social media post blaming the unpopular conflict with Iran for the GOP's drubbing.
articles.body:
USA

United States Vice President JD Vance publicly broke from President Donald Trump's defence of the Iran war Wednesday after the Republican Party's deep losses in the midterm elections, attempting to distance himself from voters' clear rebuke of the president as the vice president faces questions about his own political ambitions.

Vance, who has said he would decide after the election whether to run for president in 2028, issued a lengthy social media post blaming the unpopular conflict with Iran for the GOP's drubbing. Vance said, "If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so.”

But arguing that the war was worth it is what Trump repeatedly did on the campaign trail, continued to do in interviews as election results came in and did again Wednesday morning. As he led reporters on an impromptu visit to the ballroom he's constructing at the White House, Trump said, “The Iran thing, we had to do and we continue to do it."

Trump said he spoke to Vance on Wednesday morning and, when asked about the vice president's post, he called it “good” and said, “I know how he feels about it," and “I think it was fine."

The president also said he “knew the war was going to impact” the midterm elections but again defended his actions.

Vance, who had long advocated for restraint in US military intervention overseas, was lukewarm in his defense of the conflict after Trump launched it and even became the face of an unsuccessful attempt to end the fighting.

Reason for loss is ‘obvious to almost everyone’

Vance, in his post, said that Republican voters cast their ballots for Democrats because of the war, the cost of living, America not being prioritized and the US relationship with Israel — a dynamic where he’s also sounded a different note than Trump.

“The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone," he wrote.

About 6 in 10 voters said the US made the “wrong decision” in taking military action against Iran, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 voters in the United States.

Most of those voters dissatisfied with the Iran war backed the Democratic candidate in their US House race, but the survey suggested the Iran war was not the leading issue for most voters.

Only about one-third of voters said the war in Iran was “crucial” to their vote for Congress, well below the roughly half who said that about the cost of living or government corruption.

Nearly all voters who backed the Democratic candidate in their US House race said going to war with Iran was the “wrong decision,” while roughly 8 in 10 voters who backed the Republican candidate said it was the “right decision.”

articles.title: Morocco say it remains committed to Western Sahara ceasefire as peacekeeping mission ends
articles.summary: Morocco says it remains committed to the ceasefire in Western Sahara even in the absence United Nations peacekeepers. Last week, the UN Security Council failed to agree on an extension of the 35-year-old mission after the US and Russia each vetoed competing resolutions.
articles.preview: Western Sahara Morocco says it remains committed to the ceasefire in Western Sahara even in the absence United Nations peacekeepers. Last week, the UN Security Council failed to agree on an extension of the 35-year-old mission after the US and Russia each vetoed competing resolutions. articles.body:
Western Sahara

Morocco says it remains committed to the ceasefire in Western Sahara even in the absence United Nations peacekeepers.

Last week, the UN Security Council failed to agree on an extension of the 35-year-old mission after the US and Russia each vetoed competing resolutions.

In a statement on Wednesday, Morocco’s Royal Palace said the country’s “voluntary commitment" to the ceasefire wouldn’t change. King Mohammed VI ordered officials to protect Morocco’s territorial integrity, national security and residents.

Mineral-rich Western Sahara is claimed by both Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front, backed by Algeria. Peacekeepers were deployed in 1988 to monitor a referendum that never took place.

Rabat welcomed the end of the UN Mission but Algeria expressed “deep regret.” The Polisario said it was “concerned.”

UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres also warned of a risk of escalation and urged all parties to exercise restraint.

Territorial dispute

The UN classifies Western Sahara as a “non-self-governing territory,” while critics of Morocco’s control describe it as Africa’s last colony. Morocco administers nearly all of the disputed territory, except for a narrow strip known as the “free zone” that lies east of a Moroccan-built sand wall.

After Morocco annexed it in 1975, the dispute escalated into an armed conflict that lasted more than 15 years and claimed more than 16,000 lives on both sides, according to the French Senate.

Bringing Western Sahara under its full sovereignty has been a central objective of Morocco’s foreign policy for decades. Rabat, which has secured the backing of a growing number of Western capitals, including Washington, Paris and London, refers to the territory as its southern provinces. The dispute has become a defining feature of Morocco’s diplomacy, with the kingdom often measuring its relations with other countries by their position on the issue.

The Polisario Front seeks independence for the territory, which it considers the homeland of the Indigenous Sahrawi people. Operating from refugee camps in the Algerian city of Tindouf, the movement aims to establish an independent Sahrawi Republic. Mainly backed by Algeria, Russia and South Africa, the Polisario has seen its international support dwindle in recent years.

articles.title: Japan denies seeking Myanmar’s removal from blacklist
articles.summary: Myanmar was put on the Financial Action Task Force blacklist in 2022 as the country was plunged into turmoil and civil war following a military coup.
articles.preview: Japan’s Ministry of Finance has denied pushing for Myanmar to be removed from a global financial watchdog’s blacklist after a report said last week that it was among countries supporting the removal. Myanmar was added to the Financial Action Task Force’s (FATF) blacklist in 2022 as the country was plunged into turmoil and widespread civil war following a military coup. The blacklist requires countries to apply enhanced screening to financial transactions with Myanmar to avoid money laundering and terrorist financing.
articles.body:
Japan’s Ministry of Finance has denied pushing for Myanmar to be removed from a global financial watchdog’s blacklist after a report said last week that it was among countries supporting the removal.

Myanmar was added to the Financial Action Task Force’s (FATF) blacklist in 2022 as the country was plunged into turmoil and widespread civil war following a military coup. The blacklist requires countries to apply enhanced screening to financial transactions with Myanmar to avoid money laundering and terrorist financing.

“There is no fact that the Japanese government sought to have Myanmar removed from the FATF blacklist,“ the ministry said in a statement to reporters. “Japan hopes that Myanmar will make the necessary improvements to strengthen its measures against money laundering and related illicit activities.”

Myanmar remained on the blacklist following a closed-door meeting of the 40-member global body in Paris on Oct. 30. Japan did not state at the Paris meeting that it wanted Myanmar removed, the ministry said in its statement.

It was reported on Oct. 30 that Japan was pushing for Myanmar’s removal, according to a senior Japanese government official and another person familiar with the matter. One of the people, reached on Thursday, said they stood by their comments, while the other could not be immediately reached for comment.

A spokesperson for Myanmar’s military-backed government said in a message on Saturday that various “friendly countries” were supporting its efforts to be removed from the list.

“The United States, China, Japan, India, South Korea and Indonesia recognize Myanmar’s efforts. We are grateful to all of them for acknowledging Myanmar’s current progress,” the spokesperson added, without elaborating.

South Korea’s foreign ministry said it was “encouraging Myanmar to abide by FATF duties, and closely coordinating with FATF member countries on the issue.”

The government “is making efforts to strengthen the capabilities of countries that have not fully implemented FATF standards to combat money laundering and terrorist financing,” the ministry said.

All the other countries named by the spokesperson either declined to comment or did not respond to a request for comment.

Myanmar’s military-backed government did not immediately have comment on Japan’s denial that it was pushing to have Myanmar removed from the list.

articles.title: Bustling market in Dhaka shows shift to solar triggered by Middle East war
articles.summary: From the Philippines to Pakistan and Nigeria, people are turning to solar and batteries to cut utility bills or just keep lights and machinery on.
articles.preview: A cramped market in the heart of Dhaka has become an unlikely ground zero for Bangladesh’s energy transition. Down narrow aisles crowded with shoppers and delivery workers, tiny storefronts are overflowing with rows of solar panels and batteries. Monju Hossain, a sales representative for Dongjin Group Bangladesh, said the retailer is struggling to keep up with demand, with sales jumping 50% in recent months from a year earlier.
articles.body:
A cramped market in the heart of Dhaka has become an unlikely ground zero for Bangladesh’s energy transition. Down narrow aisles crowded with shoppers and delivery workers, tiny storefronts are overflowing with rows of solar panels and batteries.

Monju Hossain, a sales representative for Dongjin Group Bangladesh, said the retailer is struggling to keep up with demand, with sales jumping 50% in recent months from a year earlier. The country’s worsening energy crisis, triggered by the war in the Middle East, is pushing households and businesses to seek alternatives to an increasingly unreliable grid.

“The blackouts in Bangladesh have gotten worse, which has increased the need for our equipment,” said Hossain, in a shop on the second floor of the Kaptan Bazar. “Demand from industrial customers has increased significantly, as they have to keep factories running.”

The busy market offers a glimpse of how the Middle East energy shock is accelerating the shift away from fossil fuels in poorer countries. From the Philippines to Pakistan and Nigeria, people are turning to solar and batteries to cut utility bills or just to keep the lights and machinery on. It’s a threat to the long-term demand outlook for liquefied natural gas, given that populous developing nations like Bangladesh have long been touted as high-growth markets for the super-chilled fuel.

The South Asian nation of 180 million has been one of the hardest-hit by the disruption to energy flows from the Persian Gulf. Load-shedding — or rolling blackouts — have stretched to as long as 18 hours a day in some parts of the country this year as LNG exports from Qatar, formerly Bangladesh’s main supplier, slowed to a trickle.

To help make up the shortfall, Bangladesh has been buying LNG on the spot market, at around triple the price of its contracted supply from Qatar, forcing utilities to hike electricity bills. That combination of higher costs and power cuts is pushing consumers toward renewables. Even Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has installed solar panels on his house, according to local media reports this week.

An informal survey of more than three dozen stalls at the Kaptan Bazar — one of Bangladesh’s biggest hubs for solar equipment — found that all of the shops have seen demand increase to varying degrees. A plunge in the cost of solar panels and batteries in recent years has made the technology more affordable for regular households, spurring sales not just in Dhaka’s markets, but across the country.

China, the world’s dominant manufacturer of solar and battery equipment, is helping enable the shift. Bangladesh’s imports of the equipment from the country more than doubled to about $140 million in the March through September period from a year earlier.

Panels made by China’s Jinko Solar and Longi Green Energy Technology are by far the most popular due to their low price and reliability, according to the Dhaka store owners. Buying a 750-watt panel, enough for a single household, costs about 15,000 taka ($121), compared to about 38,000 taka a year in electricity bills.

Adding a battery and associated equipment will quickly boost the outlay by several times, but those costs can be recouped within a decade for a normal family, Dongjin Group’s Hossain said.

The shift to solar is being abetted by Dhaka, which cut import tariffs on the equipment in September. The government is aiming for renewables to make up 20% of the power mix by 2030 and 30% by 2040, according to a local media report this week that cited Prime Minister Rahman. That’s up from just 2.5% last year.

Authorities have accepted that more clean power will reduce the country’s vulnerability to this and future energy shocks, according to Shafiqul Alam, the lead analyst for Bangladesh at the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis. The cut in solar import taxes is a help, but it’s more beneficial for high-income households that can afford to buy the systems upfront.

“For lower-income groups, they might consider models like India’s capital subsidy,” he said, referring to a program that provides households with subsidies and other payments for installing solar equipment.

Abdul Hakim began installing rooftop solar at his ceramics factory in Dhaka about six months ago. He now sees enough enthusiasm for the technology that his company is considering expanding into the energy business, itself, supplying panels and lithium batteries.

“Demand is high,” said Hakim, managing director of Excellent Ceramics Industries. The next step for Bangladeshi consumers is lithium, he said. “For the backup, they need a lithium battery.” Still, the kiln at Hakim’s factory runs on natural gas and can’t be fully replaced by solar.

The country’s textile and garments plants — Bangladesh’s top export — which supply international brands like H&M and Ralph Lauren have a similar problem. Textile manufacturing is energy-intensive, with gas-fired boilers producing steam that’s used in dyeing and finishing the fabrics.

Mosharaf Hossain, one of Bangladesh’s leading industrialists, said his clothing factory’s on-site boiler produces far more power than he could generate from solar panels on the available land, and even if he could, renewable energy couldn’t fully meet his needs.

“Solar only produces electricity, not steam for industrial boilers,” said Hossain, the chairman of the Mosharaf Group, one of the country’s biggest textile producers.

Despite solar’s unsuitability for some industries, the energy crisis is forcing companies in almost every part of Bangladesh’s economy to think about how renewables can help cut costs.

At the InterContinental Hotel in Dhaka, grid outages plunge the building into darkness several times a week, before onsite diesel generators restore power less than 10 seconds later. For guests, it’s a brief inconvenience, but it forces the hotel to burn more diesel at a time when prices for the fuel are near record highs.

The hotel is looking at installing solar panels on its roof, according to one of its managerial staff. Lithium-ion batteries could allow it to store that power and reduce its reliance on the costly diesel generators, he said.

articles.preview: The Philippine's latest inflation number is the highest since February 2023. The latest inflation number was the highest since the 8.6 per cent recorded in February 2023, chief Philippine statistician Dennis Mapa said, topping analysts' forecast of 7.6 per cent.
articles.body:
The Philippine's latest inflation number is the highest since February 2023.

MANILA: Soaring petrol prices driven by the Middle East conflict pushed inflation in the Philippines to a 44-month high of 7.8 per cent in October, the government said Thursday (Nov 5), as the country continues to struggle with a devalued peso.

The latest inflation number was the highest since the 8.6 per cent recorded in February 2023, chief Philippine statistician Dennis Mapa said, topping analysts' forecast of 7.6 per cent.

"The main reason for the rise in inflation in October compared to September is the 20 per cent rise in transport costs," he told a news conference.

The Middle East conflict has had a harsh impact on the oil import-dependent Philippines, with the peso also diving to record lows, driving up transportation costs for commuters while also affecting other costs from power generation to food transport.

The latest figures bring the inflation rate for the year to 5.6 per cent, well above the government target of 2 to 4 per cent.

"There are risks that we face ahead," Mapa said, citing the El Nino dry spell now starting to affect the country's food supply as well as rising energy commodity prices.

The inflation data was released two weeks after the central bank raised its key lending rate by a substantial 50 basis points to 5.50 per cent.

The bank said it needed a "strong monetary policy response to broadening price pressures and further upside risks to inflation".

As the peso fell to 64 to the dollar last week, President Ferdinand Marcos told Filipinos "don't panic", and blamed the exchange rate woes on the rising prices of oil.

While Manila could "do nothing" about global oil prices, Marcos said Philippine foreign exchange reserves were at a healthy level and the government had "all the tools to defend the peso".

Rising inflation has impacted the growth of the Philippine economy, which expanded by a paltry 2.3 per cent in the three months to June, the lowest since the fourth quarter of 2009, excluding the pandemic years.

Third-quarter gross domestic product growth data is scheduled to be released on Monday.

articles.title: Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war
articles.summary: The vice-president's blunt assessment of Republican election defeat marked one of the sharpest breaks with a sitting president in recent memory.
articles.preview: Vice-President JD Vance sent shockwaves through Washington on Wednesday by blaming his party's midterm defeat squarely on the Iran war, in what was widely interpreted as an effort to distance himself from President Donald Trump ahead of a potential 2028 White House run. In a carefully calibrated, 600-word statement on X, the vice-president acknowledged that Trump's 2024 voters had deserted Republicans in the midterm election. "The reason we lost is the war," he wrote.
articles.body:
Vice-President JD Vance sent shockwaves through Washington on Wednesday by blaming his party's midterm defeat squarely on the Iran war, in what was widely interpreted as an effort to distance himself from President Donald Trump ahead of a potential 2028 White House run.

In a carefully calibrated, 600-word statement on X, the vice-president acknowledged that Trump's 2024 voters had deserted Republicans in the midterm election.

"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote. "The president himself said so last night."

In interviews late Tuesday night and Wednesday, Trump had defended the war but acknowledged that it played a factor in Democrats flipping control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate.

Vance's view on the war in Iran is an open secret in Washington. While he has repeatedly backed the conflict since the US and Israel attacked Tehran in February, he has reportedly expressed opposition in private meetings with administration officials.

But those disagreements had been kept out of the public eye - until now.

Hours after Trump and the party were handed a bruising election defeat, Vance made clear that he felt the decision to go to war was a clear political mistake.

"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," Vance said.

It was a striking statement, and one with no recent precedent: it's hard to recall a similar moment in recent US political history when a sitting vice-president has so sharply broken with the president on a signature foreign policy issue.

Then came an arguably even greater surprise: Trump - who typically demands steadfast loyalty from his senior advisers - agreed with Vance that the midterms were "largely" decided by the war. He added that he would "do it again" if given the same choices.

- LIVE: Follow latest updates

- BOWEN: Trump's loss limits powers at home, but it will likely be different abroad

- THE BIG MOMENTS: Ecstatic scenes that greeted key results

- ZURCHER: Midterm carnage weakens Trump but he still wields power for now

- 'A DISASTER': Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms defeat

It was an early sign that Trump - who has prized loyalty from his advisers - may give Vance a wide berth should he choose to launch a presidential campaign.

"I know how he feels about it. I think it was -- I think it was fine," Trump told reporters when asked about Vance's post blaming the war. "I knew that when I went in, and we stopped them from having a nuclear weapon, and they will never have a nuclear weapon."

Vance's statement seemed like "a way of separating himself from Trump," said Daniel Byman, a foreign policy expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

Drawing contrasts with Trump will be a delicate balancing act if Vance seeks the presidency, Byman added.

That balance was on display in Vance's post. The vice president didn't mention Trump by name and attributed much of his election results analysis to unnamed pollsters.

Vance "put his toe in the water to see what he's going to do," Ashley Davis, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.

Beyond the Iran war criticism, Vance also offered a political roadmap that could preview a possible presidential campaign. He distilled the party's strategy to win back voters into a neat four-point gameplan: "1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel."

The list encapsulated much of Vance's worldview since bursting onto the national political scene, and read like the core argument in a future stump speech.

The BBC has contacted Vance's office for comment.

Of course, the next presidential election is still two years away. Vance is expected to run but hasn't made an official decision, and aides insist that he's still mulling it over.

It's also up for debate exactly how much Vance broke from Trump. Vance showed the message to Trump before posting it online, according to The New York Times.

Trump, for his part, could change his mind and make clear he'll brook no dissent from Vance or anyone else.

The president has been circumspect about who he'd support to succeed him as the 2028 Republican presidential nominee. Trump has praised Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio on several occasions, but hasn't said when - or if â he'd make an endorsement.

The president appears to relish the guessing game of who he'd back to carry on his political movement, even in the past floating the idea that he'd continue to a third term (which is barred by the US Constitution).

Vance's midterms missive might not be that significant in the end. Or it could have been the starting gun for the 2028 race and the battle for the post-Trump Republican Party.

articles.title: OpenAI president Greg Brockman says company could be IPO ready in 2027
articles.summary: OpenAI President Greg Brockman says the company could be ready to go public in 2027, pointing to accelerating enterprise revenue and a turnaround in its business.
articles.preview: OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman said the company would be ready for an IPO in 2027, noting that its enterprise revenue has been growing. Speaking at a Wall Street Journal tech conference on Wednesday, the executive touted how the company had been gaining ground in the enterprise market, where rival Anthropic had already successfully made inroads. In response to the interviewer’s question about being IPO-ready next year, Brockman replied, “I think so.
articles.body:
OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman said the company would be ready for an IPO in 2027, noting that its enterprise revenue has been growing. Speaking at a Wall Street Journal tech conference on Wednesday, the executive touted how the company had been gaining ground in the enterprise market, where rival Anthropic had already successfully made inroads.

In response to the interviewer’s question about being IPO-ready next year, Brockman replied, “I think so. Yes.”

“We’ve been very clear this year that we want to go public when we feel is the right time for us, and I feel extremely good about the business. I feel like we’ve made so much progress this year, and I’ve honestly never felt more confident in what we’re doing,” Brockman said.

He detailed how OpenAI’s trajectory as an enterprise had changed over the course of 2026, noting that the first and second quarters were “pretty rough.” He also admitted that OpenAI “wasn’t even in the conversation” when it came to agentic coding — an area where Anthropic’s Claude Code has gained market share.

“We had Codex, but no one was talking about it,” Brockman continued, “and I think that we just kept our heads down and executed.”

By the third quarter, activity picked up, as OpenAI saw 70% quarterly growth in its annualized revenue — something Brockman attributed to the enterprise side of the business doubling. He explained that the growth wasn’t simply the result of something that happened in the quarter itself, but rather the culmination of investments the company had been making up to that point.

Now, the majority of OpenAI’s revenue is coming from the enterprise business, which previously accounted for only around 30% of its total revenue.

“And it’s not that consumer [revenue has shrunk]…It’s been growing, but it’s the enterprise segment has really taken off,” he said, pointing to a recent partnership with J.P. Morgan Chase as one example of the type of client it’s now winning deals with.

Brockman also spoke more broadly about the lessons OpenAI learned from selling into the enterprise market as well. He said the company had come to understand that its job was to help businesses identify the most important milestones they could achieve with its AI technology, build trust with clients, and demonstrate that it was a reliable partner for the long haul.

“A year ago, we weren’t even really in the enterprise game, right? We were really perceived as a consumer company, and a lot of the companies we’d start talking to would say, ‘Is OpenAI really committed to the enterprise?’, Brockman said. “But it’s so different today.”

articles.title: Claude AI can plug directly into your bank account
articles.summary: Anthropic has a new pitch for managing your personal finances: let Claude do it instead, with a new Personal Finance feature that connects it to your bank and card accounts via the Plaid bank bridging platform. You can ask the chatbot "where did my money go this month," for example, and it'll create an overview
articles.preview: Anthropic has a new pitch for managing your personal finances: let Claude do it instead, with a new Personal Finance feature that connects it to your bank and card accounts via the Plaid bank bridging platform. You can ask the chatbot "where did my money go this month," for example, and it'll create an overview
articles.body:
Anthropic has a new pitch for managing your personal finances: let Claude do it instead, with a new Personal Finance feature that connects it to your bank and card accounts via the Plaid bank bridging platform. You can ask the chatbot “where did my money go this month,” for example, and it’ll create an overview with a breakdown of spending by category, including rent and utilities, shopping, and food. Claude can also answer broader questions around what bills are left before your next payday, if you can afford big purchases like holiday trips, and how much money you could be saving each month.

With access to your bank account via Plaid, Anthropic’s chatbot will try to explain where your money is going and what you can afford.

Its access is read-only, and with Plaid facilitating the connection, Claude doesn’t see your banking passwords and your bank doesn’t have to deal with unvetted AI bots crawling around your accounts.

Claude can’t move, manage, or invest your money, according to Anthropic, and it “isn’t designed to give investment advice.”, but it can see the bank’s name, account names, account type, the last four digits of the number associated with it, your balances and credit limits, and up to two years’ worth of your transaction history.

If you choose to give it access to all that, Claude can explain financial terms you don’t understand and answer questions about your balances and transactions.

Personal Finance in Claude is rolling out in beta this week to Claude Pro, Max, and Ultra plan subscribers in the US. Anthropic’s announcement follows OpenAI introducing a similar feature for ChatGPT in May, which also plugs into your bank accounts through Plaid. Allowing AI to have oversight into your finances might ring some alarm bells, but according to the sign-off in Anthropic’s press release, it’s just the beginning:

“Personal Finance is a first step. For life’s bigger money decisions, we think people are best served by Claude working alongside the licensed professionals and regulated firms they trust. We’re exploring how to make that possible in Claude, and we’d like to hear from banks, wealth managers, and financial services companies who want to help shape it.”
